reason: 13 distinct claims are supported by at least two independent sites, including the identification of the magnetar, the specifics of the 1998 flare, and the discovery of the stable infrared ring.
story: A dead star known as SGR 1900+14 is a magnetic monster lurking 20,000 light-years away. This 'magnetar' is a neutron star with a magnetic field trillions of times stronger than Earth’s. On August 27, 1998, it experienced a massive eruption so intense that it overwhelmed satellite sensors across our solar system. Even the shielded Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer was flooded with radiation. This blast was a giant flare—likely caused by a massive disruption of the star's crust—releasing a burst of energy that left the object emitting a pulsating tail as it spun every 5.16 seconds. Years later, NASA’s Spitzer Space Telescope discovered a mysterious 'ring of fire' seven light-years wide surrounding the star. This stationary ring is believed to be a permanent scar from the magnetar's violent past, proving that even the most distant stars can scream loud enough for the entire galaxy to hear.
angle: A starquake 20,000 light-years away was so powerful it saturated satellite detectors throughout our solar system and left a permanent seven-light-year-wide ring of fire in its wake.

claims.claim: SGR 1900+14 is a soft gamma repeater (SGR) located in our galaxy.
SGR 1900+14 is a magnetar, an intensely magnetic type of neutron star.
The magnetar's magnetic field is trillions of times more intense than the magnetic field of Earth.
A massive giant flare or burst was detected from the star on August 27, 1998.
The 1998 burst was so intense that it caused the detectors of multiple satellites to saturate or receive unusually strong signals.
The Rossi X-ray Timing Explorer (RXTE) detected the burst despite the intensity of the event.
The star has a rotation period of 5.16 seconds.
The giant flare was followed by a long pulsating tail of radiation lasting hundreds of seconds.
SGR 1900+14 is associated with the supernova remnant G42.8+0.6.
NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope discovered a mysterious infrared ring around the magnetar.
The infrared ring measures approximately seven light-years across.
The ring remained stationary and showed no discernible change between observations in 2005 and 2007.
Magnetars like SGR 1900+14 are formed from the core-collapse of massive stars at least eight times the mass of the sun.

disputed: The distance to SGR 1900+14 is disputed, with Wikipedia citing 20,000 light-years and NRAO citing 15,000 light-years; the script should use 'about 20,000 light-years' or mention the proximity to the galactic plane.

The ionization of Earth's atmosphere is only detailed in Wikipedia, whereas scientific sources focus on satellite saturation; the script should focus on the impact on space-based sensors for better attribution.

The origin of the Spitzer ring is labeled as 'unknown' in Wikipedia but as 'formed by a powerful flare' in the Newswise report; the script should attribute the flare theory to the Spitzer research team.
